newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU ministers to discuss Vilvoorde closure plans.
newsitem.headline: EU ministers to discuss Vilvoorde closure plans.

text.p: European Union Social Affairs ministers are due on Thursday to discuss efforts by trades unions and employers lobbies to agree to a code of conduct on consulting workers when firms decide to shut down operations.
The move was prompted by the much-criticised decision of French carmaker Renault to close its Vilvoorde assembly plant in Belgium, with the loss of 3,100 jobs.

Thursday's Social Affairs Council in Luxembourg is not expected to produce any decisions on the Renault affair or any other matter on the Council table but it hopes to make progress on a number of important proposals.

Ministers will discuss the controversial issue of incorporating the social protocol, which Britain has refused to sign, into the EU treaty and changing the rules so that social programmes can be approved by a qualified majority.

They will also examine a European Commission proposal for a binding EU directive to give women better protection against discrimination at work by shifting the burden of proof away from women and onto their employers.

The draft directive -- COM(96)340 -- says that once the courts have accepted a woman's claim that there is a case to answer, then it is up to the employer to prove that discrimination has not occurred.
The proposal is based on the social protocol to the EU treaty, which does not apply to Britain.

The European Parliament approved it last week with amendments. Commissioner Flynn has said he is prepared to incorporate most of these into a final version of the text which ministers are expected to approve formally on June 12.
Ministers are also due to discuss a Commission proposal to clarify EU directive 76/207/EEC on equal treatment at work for women and men.

This comes in the wake of a European Court of Justice ruling that a German law guaranteeing women absolute priority for appointment and promotion went beyond the principle of equality set out in the EU directive (the so-called Kalanke judgement).
The Commission argues that positive discrimination is compatible with the directive and only absolute and unconditional quotas are illegal.
But member states are deeply divided over the issue and no meeting of minds is expected from Thursday's meeting.
The Council will then review the work of a new advisory committee set up to monitor national employment policies and labour market trends.

Commissioner Padraig Flynn is due to brief ministers on the work of another group of labour experts, whose aim is to break the deadlock in the Council over draft laws that would allow firms to set up as European companies rather than national ones.
The European Company Statute, first proposed by the Commission 20 years ago, has been blocked by a conflict over its provisions on worker participation in company decisions.
The conflict has also blocked the proposed European Association, the European Mutual Society, the European Cooperative Society and the Fifth Company Law Directive.
The expert group, chaired by former Commissioner Etienne Davignon is due to present its final report in May.
Finally, Flynn is expected to present to ministers a Commission Green Paper, adopted on Wednesday, on ways of introducing more flexible working practices without reducing worker security.
